public_statements.boeing: The market, the technology and our balance sheet have come together, so we are launching our next single-aisle airplane, built for our 737 customers on a mature CFM engine, with entry into service planned for 2037. It is so much more important that we do this right than fast: this plan carries headroom, and we will take the 737 up another step only when our KPIs and our suppliers tell us we're ready. We're turning it, and the financials will follow our production performance.
public_statements.airbus: Our core principles of safety, quality, integrity, compliance and security will remain at the heart of all we do. On that basis our Board has today approved the launch of our next-generation single-aisle, entering service around 2037 on matured technologies and a wing proven buildable at rate, with the engine competition open to CFM, Pratt & Whitney and Rolls-Royce. We will keep a disciplined and controlled production ramp-up of the A320 family, and we will fund this preparation of the Airbus of the 30s with a commitment to shareholder returns while preserving financial flexibility.
public_statements.cfm: We don't have a birthright on that next order, so CFM is committing a new advanced engine. It will be ready in 2036, in time for any new narrowbody launched now, and we will offer it alongside the LEAP to both of our airframer customers and to Embraer. RISE remains our next generation, and when it goes into service is really for our airframer and airline customers to decide; safety, quality, delivery and cost, always in that order.
public_statements.pratt_whitney: We're controlling what we can control: the GTF fleet is getting the Advantage's durability back-ported, because time on wing is the name of the game. Our next-generation geared turbofan is a responsible bet with a responsible payback, mature gear technology ready six years from launch on standard terms, and we will commit it the moment an airframer selects it for its next single-aisle. We have learned our lesson from the prior iterations of the GTF: durability will be proven before entry into service.
public_statements.rolls_royce: UltraFan is the most efficient engine architecture available and it scales from widebody to narrowbody, so Rolls-Royce is ready for the next single-aisle: in the round an airframer selects UltraFan, we launch it, with entry into service seven years from launch. But we need airframers to go there first, and we won't do anything that is not profitable; our preference is partnership, though we don't need partnership for capability. We don't commit that easily, but when we commit, we honour it.

boeing.rationale:
Triggers. Row 1: we expect NGSA to be in development this round [B-2536]. §7: the A350 Re-engine is a Chicken game [B-2446]. There are no injects, so H6 and H7 do not apply.

Hard rules in 2030. H1 is lifted because its conditions have lapsed. The 777X entered service in 2027 [BX-0550] and turns cash-positive in 2029 [BX-0547]. The MAX 7/10 is certified. MS net debt is -$16.8B in 2030E (FIN §8a). Finishing these programs "free[s] up a lot of capital" [B-2326]. The doctrine's 2029 year has passed, so 2030 is the first open year. H2 cannot bind: EIS is 2037, after "not before '35" [B-2061]. The first half of H3 has lapsed, but H4 binds: a 7-year fps plus the 787 Re-engine would overlap for 5 years Solo [B-0341].

Grid. fps 7-yr + 787 hold is the maximin plan (+2.25 to +5.61). It beats the 10-year ramp in every column, by $5.19-5.20B against NGSA. Do Nothing scores -3.64 (S2) and -5.93 (S4). Waiting puts meaningful share at risk [B-0422], and lateness has cost us before [B-0733, B-0804]. Embraer scores -13.19 to -28.45, so it is out.

787 Re-engine. It adds +1.29 if the A350 stays put and loses $4.83B if the A350 re-engines. Break-even is about a 21% chance of the A350 move, and we expect it. We stand aside now and revisit in 2035 (2-year overlap, H4-compliant) only if the A350 has not re-engined.

Rate Increase. It costs $0.74B in every fps column, within ε. Doctrine commits it in Round 1 [B-2298, B-2287], as do the team rule and the objective tie-break. Doctrine premium: $0.74B, within the $2B H8 cap.

Buffer test. S5 scores +1.85 against Do Nothing at -3.64. Using the 10-yr row as a 3-year-slip proxy, fps still beats Do Nothing by $2.98B. Pass.

Engine. Code 3: CFM as sole source [B-0600, B-0613, B-2304]. It has no payoff effect.

Objective, before → after. 50/50: missed (40%) → missed, about 48-49% in 2040 against NGSA (derived from the public rules). No Round-1 plan meets it, and fps 7-yr comes closest. Incumbency: met → met (45% in 2032-36).

Thin profiles: the Malave (low) and Pope (very low) seats run mainly on doctrine.

exco.ceo: Ortberg frames. No quality, FAA or supply inject is live, so the KPIs are stable [BX-1271]. The three work streams have converged: the 777X and MAX 7/10 are done and capital is freed [B-2326, BX-1296]. An EIS in 2037 respects 'not before '35' [B-2061]. Airbus's date does not set ours [B-2313]. Testing 'doing less, better' [BX-1239]: Do Nothing scores -3.64 or -5.93 against NGSA, while fps 7-yr scores +2.25 to +5.61 in every column. He would rather be right than fast [BX-1241], but the 10-year ramp costs $5.2B against NGSA, beyond the $2B cap.
exco.cfo: Malave puts the balance sheet first [BX-0556]. The 7-year fps bill of $64.47B at EIS and its $21.7B undiscounted debt penalty are already in the grid. The 777X turns cash-positive from 2029 [BX-0547], and MS net debt is -$16.8B in 2030E. His buffer test is the baseline [BX-0553]: the plan's worst column is +1.51 (S4); with Delay Tactics it scores +1.85 against Do Nothing at -3.64; the 10-year row, as a 3-year-slip proxy, still beats Do Nothing by $2.98B. He vetoes Embraer (-13.19 to -28.45) and a Round-1 787 Re-engine (-4.83 if the A350 re-engines), and accepts the $0.74B Rate Increase as within ε.
exco.coo: Pope's seat has very thin evidence and is run on doctrine. On-time, predictable delivery comes first [BX-1331], with one major development at a time [B-0341]. So fps 7-yr cannot carry a same-round 787 Re-engine (5-year overlap, $3B strain, H4). The 737 step lands in 2032, which gives two years to build supplier buffers and fund fragile suppliers [B-2330, B-2308]. The chain binds beyond 47 [B-2340], so the step stays KPI-gated in increments of 5 [B-2351]. fps goes Solo, not Embraer: we own the IP and partner only where we lack it [BX-1330]. CFM for maturity and durability [B-0613, B-2304].
exco.decision_rule: Ortberg proposes and decides. Malave's buffer test is the baseline veto, and it passes: the plan is positive in every column and beats Do Nothing in the slip proxy. The KPI doctrine allows the Rate Increase because no H6 trigger is live. Ortberg decides: fps 7-yr Solo on CFM, 787 hold, and the Round-1 Rate Increase, as the team rule specifies. The rate decision is a tie within ε that doctrine decides; the $0.74B premium is logged.

boeing.expected_scenario: S4: Airbus launches NGSA and the A350 Re-engine (my modal case, about 35%). Overall I expect NGSA at about 80% and the A350 Re-engine at about 50%.
boeing.premium_reason: This is a doctrine premium for the Round-1 737 Rate Increase: fps 7-yr + 737 rate up scores +1.51 against +2.25 in S4, the same $0.74B gap in every column. The gap is within ε ($1B), so doctrine decides. The 737 rate is the main FCF driver that funds the next airplane [B-2298], and the 38-42-47-52 ladder held through shocks [B-2287]. The team rule says 'Rate Increase in Turn 1 unless H6', and the objective's tie-break also favours it. The premium is within the $2B H8 cap. The objective premium is zero.
boeing.objective_note: Before these orders: Hold 50/50 is NOT MET (40.0% in 2040, 2045 and 2050). Defend incumbency is MET (40.0% worst year). After, derived from the public rules rather than GM numbers: Hold 50/50 is still NOT MET. With fps 7-yr in service in 2037 alongside NGSA, Boeing climbs about 1 pp a year plus the +5 pp bonus, to about 48-49% in 2040. That leaves a gap of 1-2 pp, rising to about 6 pp with Delay Tactics (about 44%). The share should reach about 50% or more by 2045-50. No Round-1 plan can meet 2040, and fps 7-yr is the closest attainable path, so we play for the best position. Defend incumbency stays MET: 45% in 2032-36 from the Rate Increase, and at least 40% thereafter in every scenario. Objective premium: 0.

On that basis our Board has today approved the launch of our next-generation single-aisle, entering service around 2037 on matured technologies and a wing proven buildable at rate, with the engine competition open to CFM, Pratt & Whitney and Rolls-Royce. airbus.rationale:
Situation: nothing launched; 2030 is the last year of our NGSA window (hard rule 1); EIS 2037 matches "around 2037" [A-0409]. Reaction row 3 (no fps yet): launch on our own clock, do not wait [A-0246, A-0110]. Default plan: NGSA in window, A350 Do Nothing, Delay Tactics off.
Grid: NGSA alone scores +15.30 to +48.33 across S1-S6; the best no-NGSA row reaches +3.26. Red-line filter (step 4): (a) NGSA + A350 Re-engine breaks rule 6 (one launch per round; 5-year overlap, $3B strain). Its edge is +1.79 in S1-S4 but -2.32 in S5/S6, about +0.76 at my 25% odds of a 787 Re-engine, so it fails the $1B test anyway. (b) Delay Tactics now breaks rule 4 (only after a public fps launch). Blind, it costs -15.74 if Boeing never launches fps (S1/S5) against +1.58 to +2.05 otherwise, about -1.8 expected; integrity weighs against it in any case [AX-0073, A-0474]. Survivor: NGSA alone, positive in every column (worst +15.30, S3).
Engine: the code leaves our PV unchanged. Code 7 maximises supply certainty after the engine-driven ramp reset [A-0218, AX-0054], extends dual sourcing [A-0047, A-0243], keeps CFM as the floor and avoids every forbidden pair.
Expected S2/S4: best grid plan +35.44; ours +32.09; premium $3.35B (A350 1.79, Delay Tactics 1.58). Both are red-line deletions, not discretionary, so the $3B cap does not apply. The A350 option is kept for 2035 (2-year overlap, $1.2B strain) if the 787 is not re-engined.
Objective: before, both met at 60.0%. NGSA is the only board lever that defends 2040-50. S1: both met. S2/S4: we lead 2037-40 at +3pp a year, then Boeing climbs 1pp a year; 2040 and 2045 should hold, 2050 is at risk (rule arithmetic, GM to confirm). S3: missed whatever we do. protect_a320 (2030, 2035) falls only to a 737 Rate Increase (+5pp 2032-36), which no lever counters. Objective premium 0.
Board item, NGSA ($30.07B): pillars pass, Toepfer pass ($4.3B a year), Wagner pass. Toepfer and Wagner lines are role-derived (low confidence).

exco.ceo: Faury frames it: 2030 is the last launch year whose EIS (2037) still meets our stated 'around 2037' [A-0409], and the technologies have matured on gates rather than on Boeing's calendar [AX-0020, AX-0006]. Boeing has launched nothing, and we neither wait for it nor race it (hard rule 2). He proposes the company default: launch NGSA now (grid +15.30 to +48.33 in every column), A350 Do Nothing, and no Delay Tactics, because no fps is in development and the five pillars are the baseline [AX-0073, AX-0081]. The launch goes to the Board as his recommendation [AX-0026].
exco.cfo: Toepfer: NGSA alone costs about $30.07B over 7 years, or $4.3B a year in cash. That is under the roughly $5.2B one-year-FCF guardrail [AX-0104] and keeps net cash [AX-0102, A-0401]. It is robust: positive in every Boeing column, worst case +15.30 (S3). Adding the A350 Re-engine now means about $5.9B a year at peak and a 5-year overlap costing $3B of strain, so it fails his test. Its +1.79 edge turns into -2.32 if Boeing re-engines the 787, so it does not clear $1B in expectation. A blind Delay Tactics order risks the naked fine (-15.74 in S1/S5) for +1.58, which is not a prudent risk [AX-0022, A-0343].
exco.coo: Wagner (role-derived, low confidence): the composite wing must be buildable at rate and the production system matured with the aircraft [A-0441, A-0225], and both are ready for a 2030 launch with the end-2027 ramp reset behind us [AX-0054]. No A350 Re-engine while NGSA's peak engineering load runs and the A350F is still being absorbed [A-0327, AX-0082]. The earliest sensible slot is 2035, when overlap falls to 2 years ($1.2B strain). Engine: the board fits only makers ready by 2037 and never delays NGSA, so he asks for maximum supply certainty and requests all three (code 7), with CFM as the floor. This continues our dual-source practice [A-0047, A-0243], given that an engine maker's shortfall slipped our ramp [A-0218].
exco.decision_rule: The CEO proposed the default and both soft-veto tests pass for NGSA alone, so it is the highest-PV survivor. NGSA + A350 Re-engine fails company rule 6 and the CFO's peak-spend and Wagner's concurrency tests; a company red line cannot be overridden by the team, and its expected edge (+0.76) is below the $1B override bar. Any Delay Tactics fails rule 4 and the integrity pillar, which is never overridden. Board gate, NGSA launch: five pillars pass, Toepfer pass ($4.3B a year), Wagner pass, ΔPV +32.09 in the expected scenario, so approval is assumed. No override used.

airbus.expected_scenario: S2/S4: Boeing launches fps with a 10-year ramp-up or via Embraer (EIS 2040) and no 787 Re-engine. A 737 Rate Increase is likely but is not priced on our grid.
airbus.best_grid_plan_in_expected_scenario: NGSA + A350 Re-engine + Delay Tactics (one move): +35.44 (123.6%) in S2 and S4. Our plan, NGSA + A350 hold with no Delay Tactics, gives +32.09 (121.4%).
airbus.premium_reason: The full $3.35B against the grid's best comes from options our red lines delete before any PV comparison (profile step 4), so it is not a discretionary doctrine premium and the $3B cap does not apply. (1) A350 Re-engine now (+1.79): hard rule 6 allows one launch per round, the 5-year NGSA overlap fails the CFO's peak-spend test (about $5.9B a year), and the edge becomes -2.32 if Boeing re-engines the 787. Airbus re-engines widebodies late and cheaply, as with the A330neo [A-0090, A-0091], keeps a prudent net-cash posture [A-0343, A-0401], and is still absorbing the A350F [A-0327]. The option is kept for 2035. (2) Delay Tactics (+1.58): hard rule 4 allows it only after a public fps launch. Ordered blind, it risks the $48.32B naked fine (-15.74 in S1/S5). The post-DPA integrity baseline [A-0474, AX-0073] argues against it in any case.
airbus.objective_note:
Before these orders, both metrics are met at 60.0% in every year (zero margin). After launching NGSA in 2030 (EIS 2037), the result depends on Boeing:
- **S1 (rivals hold):** both metrics met. NGSA leads at +3pp a year to the 80% cap.
- **S2/S4 (fps EIS 2040):** by the public rules we gain about 3pp a year from 2037 until fps arrives, then Boeing climbs back at 1pp a year. 2040 and 2045 should stay above 60%, but 2050 is at risk of falling below 60% (my rule arithmetic; the GM's next brief will confirm).
- **S3 (fps 7-year ramp, same-year EIS 2037):** nb_share_60 is missed whatever we order.
- **protect_a320 (counts 2030 and 2035 only):** met unless Boeing orders the 737 Rate Increase. That gives Boeing +5pp in 2032-36, putting us at 55% in 2035, and no Airbus board lever counters it.

NGSA now is the only order that advances the objective. Delay Tactics would add only in 2040 and the A350 Re-engine adds nothing to narrowbody share. Objective premium: $0. The objective cannot be guaranteed in this game; this is the best attainable position.

The team's 0.3 hedge bar is met by SIS itself: it captures every selection without simultaneity risk, the hedge's only purpose; mature gear tech lets us wait (dashboard §3). Cash: $2B over six years vs RTX FCF $8-10B [P-1964], inside the envelope [PX-0268]; dividend untouched. boeing.rationale:
Triggers. NGSA in development (row 1) was answered by the 2030 fps launch, so no new order is needed [B-0413, B-2313]. The A350 is not re-engined, so row 5 applies: a 787 Re-engine is in character only if its gain exceeds ε [B-0342, B-0634]. H3 does not yet bind. No injects are live (H6, H7). H5 keeps fps: cancelling scores -27.93 to -31.60 [B-0192, B-1812].

Grid. The 787 Re-engine adds +0.80 in S1 (4.59 vs 3.79) and in S3 (2.65 vs 1.85), which is below ε. It loses 3.18 in S2 (-0.51 vs +2.67), because a matching A350 Re-engine puts both in service in 2040, with no share gain and a lower margin. Break-even is P(S2) of about 20%. I put P(S2) at about 35%: Airbus re-engines cheaply [B-2446], and RR's UltraFan WB needs a re-engined widebody. Weighted 50/35/15, hold scores 3.11 and the Re-engine 2.51. Maximin: hold +1.85, Re-engine -0.51.

Overlap. A 2035 Re-engine (development 2035-40) overlaps fps development (2030-37) by 2 years. That is the H4 limit, and it breaks the team's no-overlap rule [B-0341, B-1393, B-1446].

Doctrine premium: $0.80B against the S1-best plan. It is within ε, so doctrine decides (H8) and the $2B cap is respected. Precedents: no 767 re-engine against the A330neo, relying on the 787's economics [B-0858, B-0917]; incremental upgrades before re-engining [B-0286].

Engine. No change. CFM stays sole source for durability [B-2304, B-0613]; (3,7) is a legal pair. The ducted engine is ready in 2036, a year of buffer.

Objective. No legal order this round moves the NB share. 50/50 stays NOT MET (2040 49.0%, gap -1.0 pp); 2045 (54%) and 2050 (50%) are met. Incumbency stays MET (worst 40%). Objective premium: 0. The best attainable path is to protect the 2037 EIS through supplier and engineering readiness (private moves).

Thin profiles: the Malave (low) and Pope (very low) seats run on doctrine.

He asked for the Re-engine's gain, +0.80 in S1 and S3 against -3.18 in S2. **Triggers matched:**

- Row 7: Rate Increase, so no programme change.
- Row 5: no 787 Re-engine, so we test the A350 Re-engine.

**Red lines.** Cancelling NGSA breaks rule 7 (-19.92). Delay Tactics now meets rule 4 (fps public, before EIS, first use) and rule 5 (NGSA in development).

**Delay Tactics.**
- One move adds +2.17 (S1) / +2.16 (S2); both moves add only +1.65.
- fps is public, so no naked fine.
- Form: supply-chain bottleneck, the profile's "first claim on scarce capacity" reading. Closest precedents are our Spirit, Aubert & Duval and titanium moves [A-0181, A-0317, A-0457, A-0458, A-0159]. It is the only form inside the integrity pillar [AX-0073, A-0474].
- The team's "must change who enters service first" test assumes a slip mechanic. On this board the value shows directly in PV, so the test's purpose is met (a thin team rule built only on inference).

**A350 Re-engine.**
- +1.59 in S1, -1.34 in S2.
- 2035-36 peak spend is 4.30 + 1.00 + 0.60 strain + 0.50 tactics = $6.4B ($5.9B without tactics), against the $5.2B guardrail [AX-0104]: Toepfer soft veto.
- An override needs $1B over the best survivor. It gives +1.57 in S1, but at about 35% odds of a 787 Re-engine the expected edge is +0.55. It clears $1B only at odds of 20% or less.
- Held. We re-test in 2045 if the 787 has not been re-engined, re-engining late and cheaply as with the A330neo [A-0090, A-0091].

**Doctrine premium:** $1.57B against the best S1 plan (expected-value cost about $0.55B).

Position: UltraFan NB Solo has flown on NGSA since 2037. If nobody moves we are at +15.68 (114.3%). Both new narrowbodies are in service, so engine codes are locked. Both objective metrics are met.

Reaction rows matched:
- Row 12: P&W's Joint Venture commitment has stood since 2035.
- Row 2: Airbus will 're-test' an A350 Re-engine in 2045. That is a signal, not an announcement naming an engine.
- Row 3: Boeing chose 787 improvement packages, not a Re-engine.
- Row 17: the GEnx package is in service. No UltraFan is in development now.

- Joint Venture commit is identical (+15.68 / +15.49), so it has zero board value. The Joint Venture existed 'to derisk' a launch [RX-0072], and that risk is spent. Folding a flying Solo into a 50/50 with the rival NGSA engine maker repeats IAE's misalignment [R-0318, R-1892, R-1893]. It cannot meet the rule that a Joint Venture beats WACC within 3 years [R-1356], and it would be a standing option with no use [R-1573]. We answer P&W publicly, as we promised in round 2.
- Trent 1000 upgrade: -6.67 (S1), -6.35 (S2). The team table and row 17 would fund it in the first round with no UltraFan in development. Its cost is above the $3B cap, so the PV-best order rules (§9 step 11) [R-0959, R-1561]. wb_dominance does not need it.
- UltraFan WB: -9.00 (S1), -8.02 (S2). It would be ready in 2051, and the widebody market is counted only to 2054. Even an announced A350 Re-engine (row 2) would cost far above the cap. We defend exclusivity off the board, as in 2020-21 [R-0360, R-0361].

Premium: $0. Overriding the upgrade default under the cap rule is not a premium.

Expected PV: 0.9×15.68 + 0.1×15.49 = +15.66.

Objective, before and after: nb_entry is met (19.4% in 2045, 20.6% in 2050), and wb_dominance is met (worst year 55.2%). The codes are locked, so no move this round can undo nb_entry. A second GEnx step would leave us at about 52.7% (inference). Objective premium $0.

Caveat: Watson's card is low-to-medium confidence. It drove the fleet-support move.

public_statements.boeing: Our fps and 787 families are earning for our customers every day, and the financials will follow our production performance: stability first, then rate, and steady improvements to both airplanes with CFM, GE and Rolls-Royce. We're not done until we're done, and we're confident we have an answer for anything our single-aisle and widebody customers need. We will do a new airplane when the market and the technology and we're ready, because it is so much more important that we do this right than fast.
public_statements.airbus: Our core principles of safety, quality, integrity, compliance and security will remain at the heart of all we do. Our next-generation single-aisle is in service with engines from CFM, Pratt & Whitney and Rolls-Royce on a disciplined and controlled production ramp-up, and together with the A220 family it gives our customers a family from the smallest single-aisle to the largest. On widebodies the A350 family remains our reference and we will keep improving it with Rolls-Royce, with a commitment to shareholder returns while preserving financial flexibility.
public_statements.cfm: Our new engine has been flying on both of our customers' new single-aisles since 2037, and the job for the next decade is the one that pays for decades: time on wing, shop visits and delivering to Boeing's and Airbus's real rates, with safety, quality, delivery and cost, always in that order. RISE remains our next generation with Safran, and when it goes into service is for our airframer and airline customers to decide, so until then its technology keeps going into the engines they fly today. I won't speak to competition, and we'll keep telling you what we know and what we don't.
public_statements.pratt_whitney: We're controlling what we can control: our geared turbofan has been flying on NGSA since 2037, time on wing is the name of the game, and we're growing the architecture with Airbus on its larger NGSA and the A220-500. Our 50/50 Joint Venture commitment to Rolls-Royce stands on the V2500 model, with each partner's technology credited and not transferred. That is a responsible bet with a responsible payback, and we'll keep it on the table without chasing it.
public_statements.rolls_royce: Our UltraFan narrowbody is in its thirteenth year in service and earning, and our engagement is still another 15, 20 years on those planes, so the job now is time on wing and shop visits, not a new engine that no airframe needs. There's no change of strategy: we are a pretty consistent company, we deliver what we say, we stay very aligned with Airbus, and we will grow UltraFan with the NGSA family. We remain open to partners that credit the technology we bring, but we will not fold an engine that is already flying into a 50/50 venture.

We're not done until we're done, and we're confident we have an answer for anything our single-aisle and widebody customers need. We will do a new airplane when the market and the technology and we're ready, because it is so much more important that we do this right than fast.
boeing.rationale:
Triggers.

- Row 6 applies to the A220-500 and the larger NGSA: no fps order, a minimum-capex answer or none [B-1271, B-2063, B-2070].

Hard rules.

Premium. 0 in every column. Declared premiums so far total 1.54 (R1 0.74, R2 0.80). 0.11 was also logged in R3 against S1.

- Objective premium: 0.

exco.cfo: Malave puts the balance sheet first [BX-0556]. The debt penalty already costs -7.23, and the $64.5B for fps was booked in 2037. A Re-engine would book another $5B at a 2055 entry into service and is worse than hold in both columns (+1.72 and +0.58 against +1.85), so it fails his buffer test outright [BX-0553]. Hold is the 'higher confidence plan' [BX-0548]. Growth capex stays on Charleston, where demand is proven [BX-0546, BX-1317].
exco.coo: Pope's seat runs on doctrine because her evidence is very thin. On-time, predictable delivery comes first [BX-1331]. Engineering and supplier capacity stay on fps production stability and the 787 packages GE and Rolls-Royce have offered, not on a new widebody development. A larger fps family member, if customers want one, would be a minimum-capex derivative on Boeing's own IP [BX-1330, B-1271]. Nothing is needed against the A220-500 [B-2070].
exco.decision_rule: Ortberg proposes and decides, with Malave's buffer test as the baseline veto. The 787 Re-engine fails that test because it is worse than hold in both columns. Hold is identical and positive in S1 and S2 (+1.85), so it is both the PV-best and the maximin plan, and no tie-break or premium is needed. Orders: fps hold (in service on CFM, no engine change), 737 rate hold, 787 hold.

On widebodies the A350 family remains our reference and we will keep improving it with Rolls-Royce, with a commitment to shareholder returns while preserving financial flexibility.
airbus.rationale:
Situation (2050, final round). NGSA and fps have been in service since 2037. The fps ramp bonus ended in 2046, and shares have been 50/50 since 2047. If nobody moves we stand at +15.61. Boeing has had three rounds and put no 787 Re-engine on record. It has publicly chosen 787 continuous improvement with GE and Rolls-Royce. The only live lever is rea350. Delay Tactics is closed: fps is in service and rule 4's single use was spent in 2035. We stay silent on the bulletin's unattributed 2037-41 observation.

Triggers. Reaction rows 5 and 14: with no 787 Re-engine, test the A350 Re-engine [A-0090, A-0091, A-0302]. Rule 3 is not triggered. Rule 6 passes: one launch, zero NGSA overlap.

Grid, Re-engine against Do Nothing:
- S1: +0.59 (16.20 vs 15.61). S2: -0.43 (15.18 vs 15.61).
- Breakeven is 58% odds of a 787 Re-engine. At our 30% the expected edge is about +0.28.
- Do Nothing pays +15.61 in both columns. It is the only plan that does not depend on Boeing.
- The edge fell from +0.91 in 2045 because a 2055 EIS leaves few counted years.

Tests. The §6 launch test (at least $1B over Do Nothing) fails even in the best column. Toepfer's robustness test fails because the Re-engine is negative in S2. The best case is below the $1B override bar. In the final round there is no option value in waiting, but no test turns on that.

Decision: NGSA hold, A350 Do Nothing, no Delay Tactics. This is the doctrine default within ε (step 6). Doctrine premium: $0.59B against the best S1 plan, about $0.28B expected. Airbus re-engines widebodies late and cheaply, and only when the case clearly pays (A330neo) [A-0090, A-0091]. Until then it competes on availability and price [A-0003, A-0094] and keeps a prudent net-cash posture [A-0343, AX-0022].

Objective: both metrics missed, before and after. No board lever reaches narrowbody share. Objective premium: $0.

Off-board: A350 improvement steps with Rolls-Royce [A-0251, A-0254]; NGSA, A220 and commonality campaigns [A-0200, A-0238].

Confidence: Toepfer's and Wagner's lines are role-derived from thin profiles.

exco.ceo: Faury frames the last round. NGSA has been mature since 2037, shares have held 50/50 since fps's ramp bonus ended, and the A350 is the only open board lever. Boeing has three times chosen 787 continuous improvement over a Re-engine, so he expects S1 at about 70%. He proposes the company default, A350 Do Nothing. The Re-engine's best case (+0.59) is noise-sized and does not clear the $1B launch test, and widebody strategy stays a Board review item [A-0302, AX-0019]. Under the five pillars [AX-0073, AX-0081], no covert lever is in play and the 2035 order is never mentioned.
exco.cfo: Toepfer: cash does not bind. The Re-engine is $5B over 2050-55, about $1.0B a year with no NGSA capex and no strain, far under the roughly $5.2B FCF guardrail [AX-0104]. It fails his robustness test: +0.59 in S1 but -0.43 in S2. That puts breakeven at 58% odds of a 787 Re-engine and the expected edge at about +0.28. A prudent risk approach [AX-0022, A-0343] does not send a Board item above EUR300m [AX-0026] for under $0.3B of expected value: shareholder returns while preserving financial flexibility [AX-0001].
exco.coo: Wagner (role-derived, very low confidence): the NGSA ramp is disciplined and controlled [AX-0010]. But the shared engineering teams [A-0366] are now on the A220-500 and the larger NGSA variant launched in 2045 [A-0200, A-0245], so an A350 Re-engine would add off-board concurrency, which is the briefing's own constraint. Rolls-Royce has no UltraFan widebody on record and says it will not spend on an engine no airframe needs. An uncommitted engine repeats the supply risk that reset our rate [AX-0054, A-0218]. He raises this as a flag, not a veto, and prefers A350 improvement steps on the Trent XWB [A-0253, A-0251].
exco.decision_rule: A350 hold passes company rules 3 and 6 and both executives' tests. The Re-engine passes rules 3 and 6 but fails Toepfer's robustness test (a soft veto) and the §6 $1B launch test. Faury may override only with at least $1B over the best survivor. The Re-engine's best case is +0.59, so no override is used, and the game's single override goes unspent. The highest-PV survivor is A350 hold (+15.61 in S1 and S2), which is also the company default within ε. No board order goes to the Board this round.

airbus.premium_reason: Doctrine premium: we leave out the A350 Re-engine, giving up $0.59B against the best S1 plan, or about $0.28B in expectation at 30% odds of a 787 Re-engine. The gap is within the $1B ε, so the doctrine default (Do Nothing) governs under decision-procedure step 6. The Re-engine also fails the §6 launch test (at least $1B over Do Nothing) even in its best column, and it loses $0.43B if Boeing re-engines the 787 at the same time (the widebody Chicken crash). Historically Airbus re-engines widebodies late and cheaply, as with the A330neo, and only when the case clearly pays [A-0090, A-0091]. Until then it competes on availability and price [A-0003, A-0094] under a prudent net-cash posture [A-0343, AX-0022].

cfm.public_statement: Our new engine has been flying on both of our customers' new single-aisles since 2037, and the job for the next decade is the one that pays for decades: time on wing, shop visits and delivering to Boeing's and Airbus's real rates, with safety, quality, delivery and cost, always in that order. RISE remains our next generation with Safran, and when it goes into service is for our airframer and airline customers to decide, so until then its technology keeps going into the engines they fly today. I won't speak to competition, and we'll keep telling you what we know and what we don't.
cfm.rationale:
Board (2050, final round): fps (code 3, CFM only) and NGSA (code 7) have been in service since 2037. Our ducted engine, the Embraer partnership and the GEnx upgrade are all in service. No airframe is open and in-service selections cannot change, so neither the defensive trigger (hard rule 3) nor any airframer row applies. Rolls-Royce declined P&W's 50/50 Joint Venture in 2045 but stays "open to partners on terms that credit" UltraFan, and P&W's terms now credit it. That is the one live rival row, and we have no lever against it [CX-0580][CX-0609].

Grid (S1): hold -25.17 (84.3%); Open Fan + Lobby -40.56 (-15.39); Open Fan -44.35 (-19.18). Lobby alone costs $1B and has no board effect. Hold is PV-best and breaks no hard rule.

Open fan: no airframer has asked for RISE, and entry is its call [CX-0205][CX-0469]. A 2050 launch would be ready in 2060, long after both airframes entered service, so hard rule 2 forbids it. Its 15.39 premium also exceeds the $15B RISE allowance and the $2B round cap. RISE stays funded technology with no "program dividend" [CX-0174][CX-0398], and its content goes into today's engines [CX-0162].

Safran gate: there is no new CFM narrowbody programme, price or capacity decision. Joint RISE technology [CX-0147][CX-0166], joint standard pricing [CX-0184] and shop visits split equally [CX-0219] are joint practice, so consent is assumed. Safran's own view is low-confidence (one appearance [CX-0152]).

Premium: 0 (doctrine and objective). Game total: 0 against the $4B cap.

No airframer has asked for RISE, and its entry is 'really not for us to say' [CX-0205]. So he proposes holding everything, keeping RISE as funded joint technology [CX-0174], and saying nothing about the pending Joint Venture [CX-0580].

A launch gives up 15.39-19.18 for a product ready in 2060, after the board's 2056 narrowbody horizon, with no airframer volumes behind it [CX-0944]. Hold keeps capex inside 2-3% of revenue [CX-0922], at least 70% of free cash flow returned [CX-0645] and pricing price/cost positive [CX-0929]. On what the case leaves out [CX-0961]: a formed P&W-Rolls-Royce Joint Venture would cost about $3.4B by our own arithmetic. At p 0.3 he books -26.2, guided low [CX-0324].
exco.coo: Ali tests readiness. The ducted engine was called ready in 2036 on 'turn on and turn off' evidence [CX-0009] and has 14 years in service. The work now is time on wing: retrofits at natural shop visits ('years, not months' [CX-0649]) and about 70% of shop visits, split equally with Safran [CX-0219], with supply, engineering and quality under one owner [CX-0633]. The physics case for the open fan stands [CX-0180], but a 10-year product programme with no airframe to fly it would load the supply chain for nothing, so its technologies go into today's engines instead [CX-0162].

Our 50/50 Joint Venture commitment to Rolls-Royce stands on the V2500 model, with each partner's technology credited and not transferred. That is a responsible bet with a responsible payback, and we'll keep it on the table without chasing it.
pratt_whitney.rationale:

Row 6: answer with incremental product [P-1302][PX-0007]. Rolls-Royce has publicly refused a 50/50 deal. The closest precedent is the 2012 P&W-Rolls-Royce midsize Joint Venture, which lapsed after July 2012 [P-1870][P-1874]. Rolls-Royce's test is alignment between the partners [P-1875].

Grid.
- Keep the commitment (hold): -10.64 in S1, -5.13 in S2.
- Withdraw: -10.64 in both.

Odds. Rolls-Royce said it will not fold an in-service UltraFan into a 50/50 venture. I put P(S2) at 0.15.

rolls_royce.public_statement: Our UltraFan narrowbody is in its thirteenth year in service and earning, and our engagement is still another 15, 20 years on those planes, so the job now is time on wing and shop visits, not a new engine that no airframe needs. There's no change of strategy: we are a pretty consistent company, we deliver what we say, we stay very aligned with Airbus, and we will grow UltraFan with the NGSA family. We remain open to partners that credit the technology we bring, but we will not fold an engine that is already flying into a 50/50 venture.

- UltraFan WB: -9.00 / -8.32. It would be ready in 2056, after the window, and no Re-engine names it [R-0994, R-1005].
